opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that this field moves so fast that it's incredibly easy to get swept along by whatever everyone else is doing. There's a new paper every day, a new model every week, a new benchmark that everybody's racing to top. If you're not careful, you end up optimizing for the thing that's measurable and visible rather than the thing that actually matters.

In research, that looks like chasing state-of-the-art numbers on a leaderboard without asking whether the benchmark still tells us anything, or whether we actually understand *why* the method works. I've spent a lot of my career on questions like "why do neural networks need to be so big?", and those questions don't come from following the crowd. They come from stopping and saying, "Wait, this is weird. Why is it this way?"

In policy, the stakes are even higher, because decisions get locked in and affect people who never had a say. If policymakers react to the hype cycle, whether it's utopian or doom-laden, they'll regulate the wrong things or miss the real harms happening right now. You have to keep asking: who is actually affected, what's actually happening on the ground, and what evidence do we have?

And in industry, it's a business question as much as anything. Companies burn enormous amounts of money and compute on things that don't move the needle for their customers. Stepping back and asking "what problem are we really solving, and what's the cheapest, most reliable way to solve it?" is often the difference between a product that works and an expensive demo.

So for me it's a discipline. The default is momentum. Stepping back is how you make sure the momentum is pointed somewhere worth going.

r001.rationale: The response says that failing to step back can lead to misplaced priorities, wasted resources, and missed real harms. It does not assert that people miss opportunities presented by the current technological moment.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's because the default pace of this field pulls you in the opposite direction. There's a new paper every day, a new model every week, and if you're not careful you spend all your energy reacting to whatever just happened rather than deciding what actually matters. That's true whether you're a grad student picking a thesis topic, a policymaker trying to figure out what to regulate, or someone at a company deciding where to put a hundred million dollars of compute.

My own experience with this came from the lottery ticket work. The question I started with was pretty simple: why do we need such big networks if we can prune most of the weights away afterward? That wasn't a question that was in fashion. It wasn't going to get me a state-of-the-art number on any benchmark. But it was a question I thought was genuinely important about how these systems work, and following it turned out to be a lot more productive than chasing the leaderboard would have been.

The thing I'd add is that "what's important" has a different answer depending on where you sit, and I think people forget that. In research, what's important is often the thing that will still be true in five years, regardless of which architecture wins. In policy, what's important is usually not the capability that's getting the most press, but the one that's quietly being deployed in a hospital or a courtroom with nobody paying attention. And in industry, it's often the boring stuff: does the thing actually work for the customer, can you run it reliably, is it worth what it costs. Those three groups talk past each other constantly because they haven't stopped to say out loud what they're optimizing for.

So I think stepping back isn't a luxury. It's the only way to avoid spending years on something that turns out not to matter. And the cost of not doing it is high precisely because the field moves so fast. If you're running in the wrong direction, speed doesn't help you.

r001.rationale: The response says failing to step back can lead people to spend years on work that does not matter, but it does not assert that they miss opportunities presented by the current technological moment.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s very easy to get caught up in the next thing in front of you. If you’re a researcher, it’s the next paper deadline. If you’re in industry, it’s the next release. If you’re in policy, it’s whatever issue suddenly needs an answer this week. Those pressures are real, but they don’t necessarily point you toward the most important problems.

You can get very good at making progress against a particular metric without asking whether that metric still captures what you care about. What are we trying to accomplish? Who is going to benefit? What would actually change if we succeeded? Those questions deserve time, even when there isn’t an immediate deliverable attached to them.

And that’s one reason it helps for people across those communities to talk. Someone outside your day-to-day work can ask a very basic question that makes you realize you’ve been taking a pretty consequential assumption for granted.

r001.rationale: The response says day-to-day pressures can distract from important problems, but it does not say that failing to reconsider what matters causes people to miss opportunities in the current technological moment.

sol-6.1.text:
Because it’s very easy to get caught up in whatever is immediately in front of you. In research, there’s always another experiment to run or another paper deadline. In industry, there’s a product to ship. In policy, there’s an issue that needs a response. Those pressures can keep you busy without necessarily keeping you focused on the things that matter.

I think you have to periodically ask: What are we actually trying to accomplish? Who benefits if we succeed? And would answering this question change what we do? That last one is especially useful, because an interesting question isn’t always an important question. You need room for curiosity, but you also need to be honest about the connection between your work and the outcomes you care about.

r001.rationale: The response says immediate pressures can keep people busy without focusing on what matters, but it does not state that this causes them to miss opportunities in the current technological moment.
